transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-10 14:00 PST | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM), Daniel (CTO Cerulean), Priya (Platform Eng), Alex (SRE), Marisol (Security)

Summary: quick intake to size reserved GPUs, discuss isolation and burst/failover. Primary drivers: predictable latency during spikes, data encryption in flight & at rest, ability to run private control plane.

Topics: reserved capacity sizing, tenant isolation (node fencing/hyperplane), burst windows and pre-warm/hotpool, telemetry & tracing, KMS integration, contract terms for burst pricing.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hi everyone — thanks for the time. quick intro, i'm Maya AE, with Liam our SE and Sofia on CSM. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Daniel (Cerulean): Good thanks, yeah we wanted to use this to align on what we need for dedicated capacity. we've been testing open models in prod and spikes are killing our costs and latencies.
[00:22] Priya (Cerulean): yeah, hi, priya here — we run inference for our customer chat features, typical batch size small but we see 3–4x traffic spikes during promos.
[00:31] Liam (Redwood SE): great, can you quantify those spikes? qps, concurrent requests, and desired p99s? even ballparks help.
[00:39] Priya: ballpark — baseline 120 QPS across a handful of endpoints; spikes up to ~480 QPS for 10–15 minutes, sometimes longer. p99 target 450ms for short responses, 800ms for longer ops.
[00:55] Alex (SRE): another constraint — we need per-tenant isolation; some customers are regulated and can't share inferencing nodes with others.
[01:04] Maya: ok that pushes toward dedicated pools with tenant fencing. we offer dedicated GPU pools where you can carve isolated slices or single-tenant nodes. there are tradeoffs on utilization.
[01:13] Daniel: can you explain how isolation works? is it VM-level, node-level, or process-level? we want to avoid noisy neighbor at hardware PCIe level.
[01:23] Liam: short answer: we support several isolation topologies. single-tenant nodes give full hardware isolation; fenced tenants on shared nodes use runtime-level partitioning plus kernel-level cgroups. there are pre-warm warm-pools we call hotpool for fast spin up.
[01:37] Priya: hotpool? how sticky is hotpool — like will you keep a model hot for us on N GPUs?
[01:44] Liam: there's hotpool/hot-node prewarm. you can reserve a warm-pool of N GPUs that keep KV cache and weights resident; warm-pool keeps models warmed for low latency. sticky-ness depends on your commitment level and prewarm SLA. during bursts, warm-pool to prewarm more nodes.
[01:57] Marisol (Security): we're also strict on encryption. we need KMS integration and HSM-backed keys, and audit logs for everything. SOC 2 plus some country residency.
[02:08] Sofia (CSM): we can provide our SOC 2 pack and a KMS integration guide; for HSM we support customer-managed keys via KMS providers and HSM partners.
[02:17] Daniel: ok nice. on burst pricing — we don't want to pay full reserved price for occasional spikes. how does Redwood handle burst capacity?
[02:27] Maya: typical model — reserved commit covers baseline throughput at lower unit cost; bursts above commit can be covered by burst capacity at a defined uplift. we also have transient preemptible nodes for deep bursts.
[02:37] Priya: what's the uplift? and how fast can you activate burst nodes — we need <30s ideally.
[02:44] Liam: uplift depends on contract and commitment. example: reserved units at base price, bursts billed at 1.6–2.2x depending on node type and peak commitments. activation: warm-pool nodes are instantish, adding new cold nodes can be 40–90s; with prewarmed hotpool we can target <20–30s for transitions.
[03:02] Alex: that's borderline — some of our SLAs are strict for certain endpoints. is there automatic fallback to a smaller model to keep latency if capacity is saturated?
[03:12] Liam: yes, you can configure smart routing policies: fallback to quantized model, smaller model, or route to another region/dedicated pool. Redwood supports rollouts and automatic fallback policies.
[03:22] Daniel: do fallbacks change output quality a lot? we need to monitor quality regressions.
[03:28] Sofia: we tie regressions to prompt sets and run continuous evals; we can alert on quality drift when fallbacks are used. we'll show examples in the benchmark.
[03:35] Priya: what about private deployment? we prefer private control plane in our VPC, but still want Redwood to manage the runtime. is that possible?
[03:44] Maya: yes — Redwood Private: customer VPC with a private control plane and dedicated nodes. options for on-prem too if you need air-gapped. note that some of the deepest telemetry and auto-scaling features are limited in air-gapped setups.
[03:58] Marisol: for private, how do audits and logs surface to us? we need immutable audit logs and token-level usage for billing and compliance.
[04:07] Liam: we export audit logs to your SIEM, provide token-level cost breakdowns in the Console, and support sustained retention add-ons. For immutable logs we can integrate with your log storage and write-once policies.
[04:18] Daniel: sounds good. curious about network topology: does Redwood require peering, or can we use private link endpoints?
[04:25] Maya: both. we support VPC peering, PrivateLink, and dedicated interconnects depending on region and cloud. we also support customer-managed NAT gateways for egress control.
[04:37] Priya: latency to our app region (us-west-2) is critical. do you have benchmarks for 8k context models on A100s?
[04:45] Liam: we have perf profiles, but real numbers depend on sequence-length distribution. we can run a customer-facing benchmark POC with your exact prompt shapes. that will give more realistic token throughput and p99 numbers.
[04:57] Marisol: on encryption at rest, can we bring our own keys (BYOK)?
[05:02] Maya: yes BYOK supported via KMS; for HSM-backed keys we work with several partners. we can include KMS integration steps in the onboarding doc.
[05:10] Daniel: if we do dedicated, what's the minimum commit? we are a mid-market team, not huge yet.
[05:16] Maya: minimum varies by region and GPU type; in us-west typical minimum is 4–8 A100-equivalent GPUs per pool. we can structure a graduated ramp and a hybrid option: smaller dedicated plus hosted overflow.
[05:28] Alex: what about failover — if dedicated pool goes down, how does Redwood route to hosted and what are RTOs?
[05:36] Liam: automatic failover to hosted or another pool can be configured; RTOs depend on warm-pool size and distance to target region. for strict RTO you keep a small hot spare in another region or use hybrid routed capacity.
[05:47] Priya: operationally, we want runbooks. who owns incident remediation? us, Redwood, or shared?
[05:53] Sofia: standard is shared-responsibility. Redwood handles infra and runtime; you own application-level retries and routing. we provide runbooks and on-call escalation paths, and enterprise plans include SRE support windows.
[06:05] Daniel: competitor question — we evaluated self-hosted because of cost but operational overhead is killing us. can Redwood reduce ops burden?
[06:12] Maya: that's the goal — unified API, managed autoscaling, and operator-grade logs. plus our Optimize tooling suggests batching/quantization to reduce cost.
[06:20] Priya: can we test quantized variants in the POC? some customers are sensitive to outputs.
[06:25] Liam: yes, we'll include quantized and FP16 variants in the benchmark and measure quality delta vs latency/cost.
[06:32] Marisol: question on compliance: do you support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning?
[06:37] Maya: yes SAML/SSO and SCIM are supported. we also have RBAC and token scoping.
[06:42] Daniel: timeline — we're aiming for an initial pilot within the next 3–4 weeks and possibly contract by quarter end.
[06:49] Maya: good, we can aim to run a 2-week POC starting next week if you can share dataset and QPS windows.
[06:56] Priya: we can prepare a small representative traffic dump and the top 10 prompt families. we'll also provide acceptance criteria (p99, degradation thresholds).
[07:05] Maya: action items recap — i'll share pricing and draft addendum; Liam will send benchmark plan; Priya will send traffic and SLA numbers; Marisol will send security checklist.
[07:14] Daniel: one last nit — how are preemptible nodes handled for performance-sensitive customers? we don't want preemptibles to be used for important endpoints.
[07:21] Liam: preemptibles are optional and used only for non-critical overflow. you can tag endpoints as critical and exclude preemptible routing.
[07:27] Alex: good. also, what telemetry do we get for token-level costs per route?
[07:31] Sofia: Console gives per-route token and latency breakdowns and we can push the export to your billing system.
[07:37] Maya: ok if there are no other questions we'll wrap. thanks everyone.
[07:40] Daniel: thanks, appreciate it. looking forward to the pricing and benchmark plan.
[07:44] (end)

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard acronyms: "K V cash" instead of "KV cache" seen at 01:44, "sock two" for SOC 2 at 02:17, speaker labels sometimes overlap.

References mentioned: Redwood Private architecture doc (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/private), Dedicated pricing deck (to be shared), Benchmark template (to be attached).
